standfirst: Retired national athletes are recruited into a police unit, which is a great premise and a sixteen episode problem. The loop is visible by the fourth hour: the team fights, the team loses badly, the hero absorbs another injury nobody with his diagnosis would survive, the team fights again. The action is well staged and the cast is better than the script. These picks deliver the same unit of misfits and violence without the repetition.

picks.why: The same appetite, in ten episodes with nothing wasted. Three unremarkable middle aged men who turn out to be lethal, a linear plot with a real clock, and comedy that comes from the group rather than from mugging. Difference: it is a single rescue story rather than a case of the week unit, and there is no romance and no sports angle at all.

The best version of righteous violence played for laughs. A mismatched team, a corrupt local power structure, and fights choreographed as comedy without ever feeling weightless. Same pleasure in watching an unlikely crew embarrass professionals. Difference: it is forty episodes of broad farce with no illness plot and no tragedy underneath, so the tone never lurches the way Good Boy's does.

For the unit of specialists solving what the system will not, on a weekly schedule. Same satisfaction, delivered more efficiently, with disguises and a reliable beating in every episode. Difference: it is pulp with no interest in the personal cost to its team, where Good Boy keeps insisting its hero is dying and then not letting it matter.

The 2026 version of the same idea at neighbourhood scale: a former criminal applying professional skills to an ordinary institution, with comedy and competence in equal measure. Difference: twelve episodes, no police procedural spine, and the antagonists are a residents association, so the violence is occasional rather than the point.

If what you liked was a team assembled around one very capable outsider, with a building full of people worth defending. Same tonal swing between slapstick and brutality. Difference: it is a black comedy with cartoon logic and a lawyer's mind, so the physical stakes are never real, and it is much funnier on purpose.

For the sports half rather than the police half. Athletes, coaching, the mechanics of competition treated with genuine affection. Difference: no crime, no action and no jeopardy of any kind. It is a family comedy about badminton, and it is the gentlest thing on this page by a wide margin.

against.title: Flex X Cop
against.why: The default pairing for a light Korean police series with an unconventional recruit. It is a straight procedural comedy with a chaebol detective, tighter and less ambitious, and it never pretends to have a tragedy in it. Anyone who came to Good Boy for the emotional stakes will find it hollow, and anyone who came for the comedy will find it better.

against.title: Mercy for None
against.why: Paired for the action, and the action really is in a different class. It is seven episodes of noir with no jokes, no team and no hope, built to hurt. Good Boy is a hangout show with fight scenes. Following one with the other only makes the writing here look worse.

against.title: Bloodhounds
against.why: Suggested because both put athletes at the centre of a fight. That is eight episodes about two boxers and a loan shark, and its subject is a friendship rather than a unit. If the ensemble is what you wanted, two people will feel thin, and if the choreography is what you wanted, Good Boy is the weaker show.
